title: Beef Carcass and Offal Inspection Process

lessons.title: Working the beef line station by station
lessons.html:
The beef inspection line in practice

In this work experience module you inspect cattle on a working line under the supervision of a qualified meat inspector or veterinarian. The aim is to become fast, accurate and consistent without cutting corners. Most beef lines have three inspection stations: head, offal and carcass.

Head station

  • Check the head tag or number matches the carcass.
  • View lips, gums and tongue; palpate the tongue.
  • Incise the submandibular, parotid and retropharyngeal lymph nodes.
  • Incise the cheek (masseter) muscles for beef measles.
  • Sterilise the knife and wash hands as needed.

Offal station

  • Lungs: view, palpate, incise bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes.
  • Heart: view, open and incise the muscle for measles.
  • Liver: view, palpate, incise the bile ducts for fluke; view the portal lymph nodes.
  • Spleen, stomachs and intestines: view, and check the mesenteric lymph nodes.

Carcass station

  • View the outside and inside of both sides.
  • Check pleura, peritoneum, diaphragm and kidneys.
  • Look for bruising, abscesses, contamination and abnormal colour or smell.

Building a routine

Experienced inspectors use the same order every time. This makes it hard to forget a step, even late in a long shift. Practise the routine slowly at first, then increase speed only when your mentor confirms you are doing every step. If the line is too fast for you to complete the procedure, ask for it to be slowed or stop the line according to the abattoir's rules.

Safety: keep your free hand behind the knife, wear the protective glove your procedure requires and keep knives sharp. Many injuries happen when tired workers rush.

lessons.title: Common beef findings and how to deal with them
lessons.html:
What you will see most often

On a South African beef line some conditions come up every day. Learn to recognise them quickly and apply the right action.

FindingWhereUsual action
BruisingCarcass, often hindquarter and backTrim; record for farmer and transporter feedback
Liver flukeLiver bile ductsCondemn liver
Liver abscessesLiver, common in feedlot cattleCondemn liver; check carcass for spread
Pneumonia or pleurisyLungs and chest wallCondemn lungs; strip affected pleura
Hydatid cystsLiver and lungsCondemn affected organs
Beef measles cystsCheek muscles, heart, tongue, diaphragmDetain for veterinarian
Tuberculosis-type lesionsLymph nodes, lungsDetain; report to veterinarian
Contamination with gut content or hairCarcass surfacesTrim

Detention procedure

  1. Mark the carcass and all its parts with a detained tag.
  2. Move them to the detention rail away from passed meat.
  3. Tell the veterinarian or senior inspector what you found and where.
  4. Do not trim or remove evidence before the final inspection.
  5. Record the final judgement.

Consistency

Two carcasses with the same condition must receive the same judgement, whoever the owner is. Inconsistent judgements cause complaints from producers and undermine trust in inspection. Check difficult cases with your mentor so you learn the standard.

lessons.title: Records and feedback in beef inspection
lessons.html:
Why records matter

Every finding on the beef line becomes information. Abattoir records show which conditions are found, on which farms and how often. They are used for disease surveillance by state veterinary services, for audits under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and for feedback to producers.

What to record

  • Date, carcass number and producer or lot.
  • The condition found and the part affected.
  • The judgement: passed, trimmed, partially condemned, detained or totally condemned.
  • The weight or number of parts condemned where required.
  • Notifiable diseases and when they were reported.

Using the data

A feedlot sending cattle with many liver abscesses may need to look at its feeding programme. A farm with many fluke livers may need to improve fluke control in wet camps and vleis. High levels of bruising point to rough handling, poor loading ramps or overloaded trucks. When you give this feedback through the abattoir, farmers can reduce losses, which also improves the value of their cattle.

Your work-experience evidence

Keep a daily log of the number of cattle you inspected, the stations you worked and the conditions found. Ask your mentor to observe and sign off when you can do each station independently. Include examples of detentions and what the final judgement was, because these show your growing judgement.

Key points

  • Follow the same inspection order at the head, offal and carcass stations every time.
  • Never speed up by skipping steps; ask for the line to slow if needed.
  • Detain carcasses with all their parts and do not remove evidence.
  • Give the same judgement for the same condition, whoever the owner is.
  • Records support disease surveillance, audits and farmer feedback.
